title: Your Monsoon Survival Kit: What Every NRI Needs to Know Before Landing in India This Summer
excerpt: From dengue prevention to water safety and gut health, a practical guide for diaspora travellers navigating India's rainy season — when familiar cities become unfamiliar health minefields.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Monsoon season in India increases risks of dengue, malaria, and waterborne diseases for returning NRIs.
  • Pack DEET mosquito repellent and wear protective clothing to avoid mosquito bites.
  • Drink only sealed or boiled water and avoid ice to prevent gut issues.
  • Humidity during monsoon can lead to fungal infections; carry antifungal powder for prevention.
  • Schedule a travel medicine consultation before departure to ensure vaccinations and medications are up to date.

Every summer, millions of NRIs pack their bags for the annual India trip — wedding season, family reunions, Ganesh Chaturthi, or just that overdue visit to ageing parents. But if your flight lands between June and September, you are walking into monsoon season, and your immune system, acclimatised to Western sanitation standards, may not be ready for what awaits. India's monsoon brings welcome relief from 45-degree heat, but it also ushers in the country's peak season for dengue, malaria, typhoid, cholera, and a battery of waterborne and mosquito-borne diseases. For diaspora travellers whose gut flora and immunity have adapted to years abroad, the risks are amplified. Here is what you need to know — and pack — before you go. ## The Mosquito Threat: Dengue and Malaria Dengue cases in India spike dramatically during and immediately after the monsoon. The Aedes aegypti mosquito, which carries the dengue virus, breeds in clean stagnant water — the kind that collects in coolers, flower pots, construction sites, and rooftop tanks after every rainfall. It is most active during early morning and late afternoon, precisely when you might be out running errands or visiting relatives. Unlike malaria, dengue has no widely available vaccine for travellers. Prevention is entirely about avoiding bites. **What to do:** - Pack DEET-based mosquito repellent (20-30% concentration) from your home country. Indian brands work too, but formulations you trust matter when the stakes are dengue haemorrhagic fever. - Wear full-sleeved clothing during dawn and dusk, even if the humidity makes you want to strip down to a vest. - If you are staying in a home without air conditioning or sealed windows, insist on a mosquito net. Plug-in repellent devices (like All Out or Good Knight) provide a second layer of protection indoors. - Inspect your sleeping area: empty any water-holding containers on balconies or terraces. If you develop a sudden high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, or muscle and joint pain within two weeks of arriving, seek medical attention immediately. Dengue is treatable if caught early; severe cases can escalate to internal bleeding and organ failure. > **"Do not let wet clothes stay on your body, even if "everyone else does it." ## Your Pre-Trip Checklist Before you leave, schedule a travel medicine consultation with your primary care provider."** ## Water and Food: The Gut Battlefield Your childhood stomach that handled pani puri from every corner stall has been replaced by a gut microbiome trained on treated Western water. The most common mistake returning NRIs make is assuming they can eat and drink the way they did growing up. **Water rules:** - Drink only sealed bottled water or water that has been boiled and cooled. Filter-pitcher systems like Aquaguard and Kent are standard in most urban Indian homes; confirm yours is maintained and the filter is current. - Avoid ice in drinks unless you are certain it was made from purified water. Most restaurants in metros use purified ice, but street-side stalls do not. - Brush your teeth with bottled water for the first week while your system adjusts. ![Ganesh Chaturthi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Ganesh_Chaturthi_Festival_%28247%29.jpg/3840px-Ganesh_Chaturthi_Festival_%28247%29.jpg) **Food rules:** - Eat freshly cooked, hot meals. The monsoon's humidity accelerates bacterial growth in food left at room temperature. - Avoid raw salads and cut fruit from street vendors. If you crave chaat, choose stalls with high turnover and freshly prepared batches. - Introduce street food gradually — do not go from a week of home-cooked dal-chawal to a full Chandni Chowk crawl on day two. Carry oral rehydration salts (ORS packets) and a course of ciprofloxacin or azithromycin prescribed by your doctor before departure. Traveller's diarrhoea is not a matter of if but when, and having antibiotics on hand can save a day of misery — or a wrecked itinerary.
Essential Pre-Trip Checklist
›Schedule travel medicine consultation.
›Get Hepatitis A and Typhoid vaccinations.
›Consider antimalarial prophylaxis for high-risk areas.
›Pack a medical kit with ORS and antibiotics.
## Skin, Feet, and Fungal Infections The monsoon's relentless humidity creates perfect conditions for fungal infections. Wet feet trapped in shoes or sandals for hours can develop athlete's foot. Skin folds — underarms, groin, beneath the breasts — become breeding grounds for ringworm and heat rash. **Prevention:** - Carry antifungal powder (Candid or generic clotrimazole powder) and apply it to feet and skin folds daily. - Wear quick-drying footwear. Leather shoes and canvas sneakers trap moisture; rubber or synthetic sandals dry out between exposures. - Shower and change clothes after getting drenched. Do not let wet clothes stay on your body, even if "everyone else does it." ## Your Pre-Trip Checklist Before you leave, schedule a travel medicine consultation with your primary care provider. Discuss: - **Hepatitis A vaccination** if you have not had one (or a booster if it has been over ten years) - **Typhoid vaccination**, especially for stays longer than two weeks or visits to smaller towns - **Antimalarial prophylaxis** if you are travelling to high-risk areas (rural Maharashtra, Odisha, Jharkhand, the Northeast) - **Prescription for antibiotics** for traveller's diarrhoea - **Adequate health insurance** that covers hospitalisation in India — your US or Canadian plan likely does not Pack a small medical kit: ORS packets, paracetamol, antihistamines, antifungal cream, DEET repellent, hand sanitiser, and a digital thermometer. If you wear contact lenses, carry extra solution; monsoon humidity can cause lens contamination. ## The Emotional Side There is an underreported dimension to monsoon-season visits for NRIs: the emotional weight of seeing parents age, homes deteriorate in the damp, and neighbourhoods change. Combine that with jet lag, gut trouble, and the sensory overload of Indian monsoon cities — the noise, the traffic, the flooding — and it can become genuinely overwhelming.
Food and Water Safety Tips
›Drink only sealed bottled or boiled water.
›Avoid ice unless certain of purification.
›Eat freshly cooked meals; avoid street food initially.
›Brush teeth with bottled water for first week.
Give yourself grace. Allow a day or two for acclimatisation before scheduling every uncle and aunty visit. Stay hydrated, sleep enough, and remember that taking care of your own health is not selfish — it is how you show up fully for the people you came to see. *Sources: Kauvery Hospital (monsoon health advisory), Manipal Hospitals (monsoon wellness guide), Dr. Vikas Vashisth / Silverstreak Hospital (dengue prevention), Practo (waterborne disease prevention)*
